title: 2013 AMC 10B Problem 24
statement: A positive integer \(n\) is “nice” if there is a positive integer \(m\) with exactly four positive divisors (including \(1\) and \(m\)) such that the sum of the four divisors is equal to \(n.\) How many numbers in the set \[\{ 2010,2011,2012,\dotsc,2019 \}\] are nice?

solutions.text:
An integer with exactly four positive divisors is either \(p^3\) or \(pq\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes.

If \(m=p^3\), the divisor sum is \(1+p+p^2+p^3\). The values for \(p=11\) and \(p=13\) fall below and above the interval \(2010\) to \(2019\), so this case gives none.

In the \(m=pq\) case, the divisor sum is \(1+p+q+pq=(p+1)(q+1)\). If one prime is \(2\), the sum is divisible by \(3\); only \(2010\) and \(2016\) qualify, but \(\frac{2010}{3}-1=669\) and \(\frac{2016}{3}-1=671\) are not prime.

If both primes are odd, then the sum is divisible by \(4\), leaving \(2012\) and \(2016\). The factorization \(2012=4\cdot503\) would give primes \(3\) and \(502\), impossible, while \(2016=4\cdot504\) \(=(3+1)(503+1)\) works.

Thus exactly one number is nice, and the correct answer is A .
hints: Convert the divisor sum for \(pq\) into \((p+1)(q+1)\)
